Background Research
Hull
Given the constraints of the racing environment, a 2-mile race over open water with
considerable waves from other watercrafts, it was decided that the hull design would be similar to
that of a deep-V planing monohull. The deep-V design is a variant of a planing monohull which is
specifically designed to cut through choppy water at speed. The primary feature which
characterizes a deep-V hull design is the large deadrise angle, usually between 20 and 25 degrees.
This angle is what allows the hull to cut through waves, allowing for a relatively smooth ride in
poor water conditions, which will be unavoidable in the competition.
As a continuation team, it is the team’s job to build upon the work of the previous PEP
team from Alabama. When the team met with the 2025 team, one of their first suggestions was to
use a professionally made hull. The reasons for this were that a hull created in-house would likely
contain inconsistencies or mistakes, as well as taking valuable time from other areas. With this in
mind, and the design chosen from background research, the team was able to move forward with
selecting a suitable design.
Power and Control Systems
Some of the key factors for maximizing power performance are power-to-weight ratio,
electrical efficiency, and thermal management. For a battery system, it is strongly recommended
to place the ESC as close to the batteries as possible. Long-distance wiring can cause multiple
issues, such as voltage drops and spikes that could damage the ESC and increase temperature due
to increased resistance. (Paramonov A) The battery configuration also directly affects the system's
efficiency. Increasing a system's voltage reduces the current for a given power (P = VI), improving
overall efficiency. Also, decreasing system’s weight improves the thrust-to-weight ratio, which
directly affects the amount of thrust required for the boat to reach planning speed due to decreased
drag.
Reevaluating the previous team’s resources and design of their battery system, which
consisted of twelve 6S batteries, revealed excess weight (~30 lbs.) and an inefficient design, which
affected the boat’s performance on race day. These factors led to a redesign of the battery system,
focusing on reducing weight and a simpler design solution to increase electrical efficiency.
Thermal management is also a major factor in a power delivery system. A continuous high
current generates significant heat in both the motors and ESCs, requiring an active cooling system
and regulation during race conditions. All the following factors contributed to the final system
design.
Propulsion
Per the Tide Chasers reporting, the boat had experienced major issues with the props lifting
out of the water. The team found 3 main options for the driveshaft to help mitigate this. The first
was a single straight flex shaft with a packing tube. The pros of this would be simplicity and
waterproofing, while also allowing the driveshaft to remain submerged at most speeds. However,
this design option was seen as not optimal, due to the motor system being designed for two motors.
Using only one of our motors would likely not be strong enough to effectively propel the boat.

The second design option was two angled driveshafts. This design would allow the
driveshaft to be submerged, while simultaneously being completely straight from input to output.
This design’s primary strength is its simplicity; it would be the easiest to fabricate with our given
materials. The primary weakness of this design is that it would not only destroy our hull
permanently, meaning future teams could not build their own unique propulsion designs on the
hull, but also be less effective, moving some of the propelling force in the z-direction.
The final and chosen design is an external z-shaped gearbox similar to that of an outboard
boat motor. The advantages of this design would be that it allows the output shaft to be lower than
that of the other two designs. The main disadvantages would be vibration and waterproofing. The
gearbox requires significant design considerations to minimize the components vibrating within
the housing, as well as designing an effective way to waterproof the output shaft tube. The team
turned this basic concept into a fully original design using 3-D CAD models of existing parts from
McMaster-Carr combined with wholly original housing and mounting components.
Cooling System
When deciding what to use for this crucial part of the boat subsystems, the team considered
an open cooling system as well as a closed cooling system. Based on the budget and interior space
available, the open cooling system was chosen to regulate motor and ESC temperatures. A closed
cooling system would require a heat exchanger, which the team did not have money for, and it was
advised that a closed cooling system would get the job done without cavitation or overheating.
Design and Analysis
Hull
Given the background research, the team decided to purchase the Enforcer Scarab 76”
hull. The justification for the purchase of the Enforcer Scarab hull design was twofold, firstly, a
plastic and fiberglass hull would be significantly lighter than the fiberglass and wood hull created
by the Tide Chasers team, increasing the system’s ability to move through the water. Secondly, the
design for this boat is a very deep V, having a deadrise angle of just over 25 degrees. This would
give the boat an advantage in the choppy water expected in the competition, allowing it to stay on
plane through reasonably rough water.
The main disadvantage of a deep-V design would be that due to the increased in-water
volume, there is an increased drag on the hull, thus more power is required to propel the hull. A
secondary disadvantage is that the theoretical top speed is lower due to this drag than a hull such
as a catamaran. The team has determined that it is an acceptable trade-off to get extra stability in
exchange for a bit of top speed.

When assembling the boat’s interior, maintaining proper weight distribution and stability
was the primary focus. The layout was designed symmetrically, with a 60-lb ballast positioned at
the center. Key components like the battery, kill switch, fuse, ESC, water pump, and motor were
evenly distributed on both sides of the ballast. This mirrored configuration ensures balanced mass
across the boat’s horizontal axis and supports efficient operation during the race.

needed within the housing. Flanged ball bearings were chosen to radially support the shafts within
the housing, with shaft collars to prevent displacement of the shafts from excessive axial
forces. The axial load on the shafts was determined from the necessary propulsion required to

The modeling began with the assembly of the z-drive components. Using the
specific component files, as provided by McMaster-Carr, a working 3D-model of the internal
components of the z-drive was created in SolidWorks to be used as a reference and proof-ofconcept. Once the internal system of the z-drive was designed and modeled, the housing for the
system was designed. The housing design had to first prioritize the fit and form of the internals:
ensuring the bearings were properly supported and secured while allowing the rest of the
components to rotate freely. Once the internal surface of the housing was designed, the external
surface was created to maintain a hydrodynamic profile while allowing for ample surface area to
fasten the hardware required to hold the z-drive together. The model also had to include a solution
to the angled transom of the hull on which the z-drive is to be fastened to. Mounting plates were
added to the design to allow the z-drive to remain horizontal while allowing for the adhesion to an
angled surface.

Electrical efficiency was also improved by decreasing the length of wiring needed and
upgrading from 10-gauge to 8-gauge wire. The previous team’s design required an excess of over
2 feet of wiring between the batteries and ESCs. This new design reduces voltage spikes and losses,
and improves reliability. The electrical circuit includes a 200A fuses and an external kill switch
that comply to the PEP 2026 safety requirements. The 200A Hobbywing ESCs being reused has a
Bluetooth option that lets the user regulate the current via a mobile app. This app also displays live
throttle %, RPM, ESC voltage, current, and temperature. This will ensure that the motors do not
overheat during testing and race conditions. Connecting the battery to the ESC are XT90
connectors to minimize resistance for a high current connection.
The auxiliary system contains two 12V water pumps and one 12V bilge pump powered by
a 12V 5200mAh rechargeable battery. Each water pump draws a maximum current of 3A while
the bilge pump draws less than 1A. Connecting this system with wago series connectors we can
calculate the run time with the equation above to be about 7 hours, well over the needed time
during the competition on full battery. This system both ensures thermal stability and removes any
water that accumulates within the hull. A fuse is not needed per PEP 2026 guidelines due to the
circuit being below 24V.
Control System
The control system consists of a RadioMaster ELRS controller, a 6-channel PWM receiver,
connected to the two ESCs. At the center of the control system is the 6-channel PWM receiver,
wirelessly connected to the remote controller. Each channel is programmed from the remote
control to transmit commands to the propulsion system, steering servo, and relay switch. First, the
relay switch controls the auxiliary pump circuit, which is powered by the 12V battery previously
mentioned in the power system section. This relay switch is connected to channel 5 and
programmed to the left side switch to serve as an on/off switch for the pump circuit. Next, the two
200A ESCs are connected to channels 3 and 4, which are programmed to the left joystick to control
the motor throttle. Finally, the 45kg servo is connected to channel 1 and programmed to the right
joystick to steer the rudder.
The rudder design was modified from the previous design from the Tide Chasers. The new
design is based on a standard airfoil shape, with an adaptor to fit onto the rudder connector from
the previous design. For most of the design and build process, the team believed that the previous
rudder would work for the new hull and design, but it was discovered that the rudder was slightly
too short to be used, so a new design was required. Because of this, the CFD simulation hasn’t
been run yet, but the plan is to run a simulation on the new design in the coming weeks.

was mostly reused. It was known that most of the tubbing had to be replaced due to mold, however
the pumps could be reused again. The previous team used two C1A centrifugal pumps from US

There is no build for the hull's body, as the hull is purchased, as mentioned previously. The

race conditions. All 10-gauge wires were upgraded to 8-gauge wires, simplifying the interior
design and reducing the wire length from the batteries to the ESCs. Each ESC is mounted adjacent

of the hull to improve weight distribution and stability. Kill switches are located above the batteries
and accessible from outside the boat, as seen in Figure 7. Fuses are located directly adjacent to the
ESCs reducing the wire length and high-current paths. The batteries are connected directly to the
ESCs by XT90 connectors, which were soldered.
The auxiliary system used wago series connectors to allow all three pumps to be powered
by the same battery. These connectors are mounted above the internal components to prevent water
damage.

Risk Management
Hull
The primary risk involved with the hull in terms of competition is the prospect of damaging
the hull. Compromising the integrity of the hull can lead to disaster, including the boat completely
sinking. The best mitigation strategy for this issue is to monitor the area where the boat is being
driven to ensure it is not endangered from the outside. A makeshift protective stand made of foam
from the packing material has been used to support the hull on the table while it is being worked
on in the lab and dockside. To protect the hull and components inside from moving or being
damaged, the team has created a robust and secure interior design which can protect the hull and
components from being damaged or misplaced.
Uneven weight distribution can cause the boat to lean or tip, negatively affecting
performance and efficiency. Imbalance may force one motor to work harder, increasing mechanical
stress and reducing propulsion effectiveness. In a competitive setting, this could compromise
system reliability or prevent race completion. By using a symmetrical layout and central ballast,
these risks are minimized, helping ensure stable operation throughout the competition.
By distributing the components symmetrically within the hull, the design minimizes the
risk of the boat leaning or tipping to one side. Any significant imbalance could negatively impact
performance by forcing one motor to work harder than the other, increasing mechanical stress and
reducing overall propulsion efficiency. In a competitive racing environment, such an imbalance
could potentially compromise the reliability of the system or even jeopardize the team’s ability to
finish the race.

risk they faced with their propulsion system was cavitation. An issue that only allowed their motors

pressure on the blade drops below the vapor pressure of water. This causes vapor bubbles to form,

and build phase by implementing a Z-Drive to lower the depth of the propellers in the water.

Power and Control System
Several risks were identified during the build and fabrication phase, and each was
addressed accordingly. High current draw could potentially damage the motors and ESCs, so a
200A fuse was installed to stabilize a continuous current through the ESC. Heat buildup is another
concern during intense race conditions, which is managed through a dual water pumps cooling
system and through monitoring the ESC temperature thought the mobile app. Electrical issues,
which include voltage spikes, current overload, and resistances losses, seen in previous designs,
were mitigated though reducing the wire lengths, upgrading to 8-gauge wires, and optimizing
competent locations. Initial testing of a fully charged battery pushed the motors past its maximum
RPM. To prevent this during competition, the team will monitor real-time RPM through the ESC
app and verify battery voltage with a multimeter before each practice run and the final run during
the competition. Finally, water will inevitably find its way into the hull in rough racing conditions,
so a bilge pump is installed to remove any water that enters the hull. Together, the steps to mitigate
risk will help the power and control systems operate safely during both testing and competition.
Cooling System
High temperature of internal components is a significant design risk that is needed to be
taken into consideration. To combat this the team has opted for an open liquid cooling loop,
drawing water from outside the boat. For this method to be effective, the primary concern is the
pump cavitating due to “starvation”.

because there was a decrease in flow rate from the inlet to the outlet. The flow rate going into the
inlet was approximately 4 L/min while the outlet flow rate was 2.95 L/min. Since the inlet has a
larger flow rate than the outlet, the likelihood of the inlet pressure falling below the vapor pressure
decreases. If there was a significant flow rate reduction, then there would be concerns of cavitation
occurring. However, this was a system that was used effectively by the previous year’s team.
